instances.detail: Isolated correctly ('outside of the investment, ready to draw a line in the sand?'), then ran the financial picture: cash on hand the $1,000–$2,500 band, monthly leftover the $500–$1,000 band, savings yes, credit score the 580–670 band. Missed the credit-card depth the script calls for — number of cards, available credit per card, used vs available — and never asked about crypto, stocks or investments. Still structured the $1,000–$2,500 band x 6 live and got a yes.

Opened the door correctly — 'my intention is to never take food off people's tables. If there's a way we can structure this, are you open to exploring that?' → got a YES. Then never ran the financial picture. Not one question about cash on hand, monthly surplus, credit or assets. The play was started and abandoned.

The money objection landed and no part of the play ran. No isolate, no 'should I vs how' reframe, no offer to structure it, no financial picture. Instead the rep ran a takeaway — 'go back to her' — twice. A takeaway is not in the script.

Price resistance landed twice — 'that's way out of my expectation' at 00:29:06 and 'that's out of my range' at 00:38:16 — and not one move of the open-wallet play ran. No isolation ('finances aside, nothing else keeping you from 100%'), no 'you're not in a SHOULD I place, you're in a HOW place', no offer to break it up, no permission question, and none of the six financial-picture questions. The rep's response to the first was 'Sure. All good, man. All good'; his response to the second was to re-present the $200/mo community product. This is the single largest process failure on the call.

Sticker shock was named explicitly. The rep isolated first, correctly, but then jumped straight to the solution — an unprompted 2 x the 800+ band split — without ever asking permission for an open financial conversation and without a single financial-picture question: no cash on hand, no monthly surplus, no cards, no available credit, no investments. The whole FINANCIAL PICTURE block of OC was skipped, so the rep discounted the friction rather than diagnosing it.

Money surfaced three separate times — 'I wasn't expecting it to be quite that much', 'I don't think I could swing that with Fife', 'don't make any decisions on financial things straight off the bat' — and not one move of OC ran. No isolate, no 'you're not in a SHOULD I place, you're in a HOW place', no offer to break it up, no permission for an honest financial conversation, and none of the six financial-picture questions. The rep's answer to money was to remove the price.

Isolate ran ('Money aside...'), the HOW-not-SHOULD frame ran in paraphrase ('the last thing we want is that money be the thing that holds them back'), and the break-it-up option was offered and a preference confirmed ('which one would you be leaning towards, the in-full or the split?' → 'Oh, the split'). Every one of the six FINANCIAL PICTURE questions was skipped — no cash on hand, no monthly surplus, no cards, no available credit, no investments — and the rep never asked permission for the open financial conversation. With a physician who had just volunteered 'I made too much, so I had to pay a lot' in tax, that block would have resolved the objection on the call.

Roughly half the play ran, and the half that was skipped is the half that matters most. Ran: the break-it-up offer ('Most people, man, they just put it on a credit card, but we have different in-house payment plan options if necessary'), the permission question ('I just got to understand things from a high level to see what we can do. You open to me asking you a couple of questions?'), cash on hand, monthly surplus (the under 580 band-the 670–740 band), and credit score (above the 670–740 band). Not run: the ISOLATE FIRST move, which the script puts before everything else — the rep never asked whether anything other than money was in the way, so when the real second blocker turned out to be his decision process, it arrived unhandled forty minutes later. Also not run: number of credit cards, available credit per card, used versus available, and crypto/stocks/investments. The 'you're not in a SHOULD I place, you're in a HOW place' frame was never used.

The money concern was raised explicitly and tied to instability — 'I don't really know where it is monetarily... that's definitely a concern just because of this work situation I'm going through' — and not a single move of the open-wallet play ran. No isolation, no HOW-not-SHOULD frame, no permission question, and none of the six financial-picture questions. The rep's entire response was 'And I hold you accountable to that, yeah?' It surfaced a second time at the point of decision — 'it's going to be tighter financially, but I have it' — and was met with 'I don't want you to be broke. I don't want to take food off your table. But I want it to be a bit uncomfortable.' Nine thousand dollars was taken from a prospect in an unstable job whose capacity was never once established. Note the asymmetry with the Omar M. call two days earlier, where the full financial-picture sequence ran on a prospect who did not buy.

'I didn't think it was going to be that much' is a money trigger and the OC play did not start. No isolate, no HOW-not-SHOULD frame, no permission for an honest financial conversation, none of the six financial-picture questions. What ran instead was off-script: a list of accepted payment methods, a mention of third-party financing, and an extended pitch on writing the fee off as a business expense.

Price was rejected three times with a specific counter-anchor and exactly one move of the play ran — the break-it-up offer: 'Whichever option you see there, you have the flexibility to divide over 12 months, even if it's 3 or 6, we have finance partners.' Nothing else. No isolation, no HOW-not-SHOULD frame, no permission question and none of the six financial-picture questions, so the rep never learned whether $4,000 was unaffordable or merely unattractive to a technology salesman who had just closed a good quarter. On the third push he abandoned the play and disqualified. Given that the prospect named a number — $2,000-2,500 — the distance to close was knowable and was never measured.

A price reaction did land — 'transparently, I wasn't expecting it to be this high' — and none of the play ran: no isolation, no HOW-not-SHOULD frame, no permission question, no financial-picture questions. Recorded for completeness rather than as a criticism: the prospect neutralised his own objection in the same sentence ('but absolutely respect him and his price'), money was demonstrably not the blocker, and running the open-wallet sequence on an optimizer whose objection is scope would have been the wrong move. The isolation question alone would have been worth asking, because it would have surfaced the scope objection ten minutes earlier.

objection_plays.trigger: I need to think about it

instances.detail: 'I'm going to, I guess, think about it' at 00:32:39 and 'I want to think about it a little more' at 00:39:11. The rep ran exactly one scripted move — 'when you say you want to think about it, just so I'm on the same page, what do you need to go over before making that decision?' — and stopped there. Missing: 'do you feel what we've gone through CAN get you to your goal', 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', 'when do you make a different decision', and the final 'are you sure, nothing else keeping you from being 100% in'.

Closing line was a textbook OA trigger — 'I'll have a think about it... I'll sleep on it'. The rep's full response was 'I can send you the link and if you want to do it do it if you don't that's fine.' None of the seven OA moves ran.

The best-run play in the batch so far. Four moves landed in roughly the scripted order: belief isolate ('Money aside, do you actually feel confident that if you did do it, you would get the results?'), worth test ('Would the results be worth the number?'), the blocker question almost verbatim ('So when it comes to doing your consideration, what specifically is coming up? Is it a logistics thing?'), and the all-in check ('is it a case where this is something that I'm going to do, I just need to get the money? Or is there still a little bit of a concern in between?'). It produced a real diagnosis — a tax bill — rather than a stall. What did not run were the three identity moves: 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', 'the way you've been approaching this brought you here', and 'that man you want to be, how does HE decide right now?'. Ends in a deposit, not a decision.

Triggered three times and played through at length, arguably well past its useful life. Ran: the direct probe ('the only question that you need to ask yourself in this moment, why am I not moving forward right now?'), the callback to his own words ('from earlier in our conversation, you said to me specifically, because I noted it down, that you know within yourself that you can't continue like this'), the deposit fallback borrowed from Objection B, and a heavy version of the deciding-not-thinking frame ('Whenever anyone says they need to think about it... it's really, really low probability that we ever hit back from them'). Not run: 'Do you feel what we've gone through CAN get you to your goal?' and 'That man you want to be — how does HE decide right now?', which are the two moves that would have worked on a prospect this identity-driven. The play was run to completion and then continued past the point where the prospect had disengaged.

'I want like a day to think about it' triggered nothing scripted. In fairness the prospect compressed his own timeline to ninety minutes unprompted, so the practical cost was low — but no move ran, and the two doubts he had actually voiced were left on the table going into that ninety minutes.

Triggered twice — 'I would just want to sit and think which program' and later 'I just also now need to sit and think if I want to really jump into a program like this.' Ran: the isolating probe ('why do you feel like you need that in order to make [a decision]?'), the do-it-to-know-it reframe ('the best way for you to understand if something's actually going to work is to actually do it'), and the $1,200 trial as a risk-reducer. Not run: 'do you feel what we've gone through CAN get you to your goal', 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', and 'that man you want to be, how does HE decide right now' — which was the strongest available line given how much identity material Phase 3 had produced. The rep then stopped and disqualified rather than continuing, which was the right judgement even though it scores as an abandoned play.

The trigger landed twice and cleanly — 'I'd have to consider it' at 00:06:46 and 'Something I got to think about for sure' at 00:10:55 — and not one move of the play was attempted. The complete response was 'Okay. No worries, brother. I mean, we're always going to be here.' No 'do you feel this can get you to your goal', no 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', no 'what's actually coming up that's preventing you from getting started', and no attempt to book a next contact. Given the prospect has a hard, dated deadline three months out, 'what's your plan between now and selection?' was available and free.

'I need to sleep on it' and 'I just need some time to process it all.' One scripted probe ran — 'what else do you kind of need to think of before making your decision?' — and the rep then booked Wednesday. None of the deciding-not-thinking sequence was attempted. Worth noting that the prospect had pre-empted it explicitly and the rep respected the boundary: 'I wouldn't make a decision now. And I think if you tried to get me to, I'd probably say, all right, I won't do it. Then I'd probably just go.' Given that, stopping was almost certainly the right call and the partial score reflects the script rather than the judgement.

'No, I want to take a look at it... I need to see.' No play ran; the rep accepted immediately with 'Sure. Any questions that you need me to answer?' Recorded for completeness rather than as a criticism — this was a deferral on a $200 subscription after the rep had already disqualified him from the main product, and pressing would have contradicted the position he had just taken.

'Let me do a little forecasting and see where things are' is the trigger. No move ran; the rep went straight to channel logistics and agreed to wait until morning. To his credit he asked a clean expectation-setting question — 'would you get back to me within the next three hours or would it be tomorrow?' — but that is call management, not the play.

The call ended on a textbook OA trigger: 'I'll think about it all. Okay, I'll think more in-depthly about this all.' Not one of the seven moves ran — no 'do you feel what we've gone through can get you to your goal', no 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', no 'are you sure, nothing else keeping you from being 100% in'. The rep replied 'we're always going to be here' and ended the call.

'Hopefully the next 24 hours' is the delay. The rep asked the right scoping question — 'How long do you feel like you really need to actually make the decision on it?' — and closed the loop with a $100 refundable deposit to hold the slot, which is a real commitment device. None of the seven scripted OA moves ran; the deposit did the work instead.

The prospect said it almost verbatim: 'it might not be the right time for me personally.' That is the exact Objection D trigger, and the script supplies six responses for it — 'things never slow down', 'when does it actually become the right time?', 'the longer you wait the harder this becomes'. The rep ran none of them. He said 'let me go back to the team' and booked tomorrow.

A textbook timing trigger: 'I'm three weeks out from my next marathon... three weeks out from a marathon, I'm not doing anything different.' No move ran. The rep did not ask 'when does it actually become the right time', did not point out that the prospect has three marathons booked this year so the window never opens, and did not use 'what if all you had to do was show up'. Instead he proposed the deferral himself: 'would it make sense to potentially revisit this and have myself message you around that three-week mark?'

The timing objection was raised in substance and early — 'it's my working hours that are so irregular. They kind of discourage me from committing to a program' — supported by the detail that every coach he has approached wanted a fixed weekly slot. The rep answered it, but with the offer's features rather than the play: 'we want the next program you enter to be the final one for you... it being adjusting to your life, not the other way around', then the 30-minute session length and the 5-10 minute mobility block. None of the scripted moves ran — no 'things never slow down, when does it actually become the right time', no 'the longer you wait the harder this gets', no 'what if all you had to do was show up and everything else was handled', which was the single most on-point line available and was never used. It resolved anyway because the efficiency reframe genuinely addressed his stated blocker.

A genuine timing conflict was raised alongside cost — a 10-day Japan trip departing the 5th plus further travel. No OD move ran. The rep instead dissolved it operationally by booking onboarding for the 4th and using the holiday as build time, which was the better answer here and worked; recording it as a miss reflects that no scripted play was used, not that the handling was wrong.

Timing was the stated blocker — Canadian tax season and a large bill just paid. A single OD-shaped move appeared, garbled in the transcript ('the way I see it is that, you know, it's going to be a big cliff today and next week'). None of the durable OD moves ran: no 'things never slow down, when does it actually become the right time?', no 'the longer you wait the harder this gets', no 'what if all you had to do was show up and everything else was handled'.

Timing was explicitly part of the blocker — 'some months are good and it's not an issue, and some months you're like oh how am I gonna make all this work' and 'I recently just restarted my business'. No OD move ran. Nothing on 'things never slow down', nothing on 'when does it actually become the right time', nothing on the cost of waiting. The rep instead accepted the timing frame and built a product around it.

'I think that the better move for me is to just focus on getting a job' is OD in substance and no move ran. Arguably correct restraint here — 'things never slow down' is not an honest answer to redundancy — but recorded as a miss because the play was not run and nothing replaced it except a second attempt at financing.

A clear timing deferral at 00:50:25: 'maybe in four or five months, say, hey, Farooq, I'm ready to do that... I don't think this is a decision like just right away.' None of the OD moves ran. No 'things never slow down', no 'when does it actually become the right time', no 'the longer you wait the harder this gets'. This prospect had the single most usable version of that argument available — a 230 km race in November and a build-up already underway — and it was never used. The rep instead treated the deferral as a pricing problem.

The prospect explicitly deferred on timing: 'we're getting right into golf season, and that's going to be very expensive. So I may have to follow up with you guys for winter.' None of the OD moves ran — no 'things never slow down', no 'when does it actually become the right time', no 'the longer you wait the harder this gets', which was unusually available here given a pending ankle surgery and a stated 10-year cycle. The rep went straight to money instead.

A genuine timing conflict — a divorce in progress, a house to sell, condo deposits pending. One OD-shaped line ran: 'if there's a cliff to climb, or if there's a cliff to jump off today, you're gonna have to jump off it tomorrow too.' Nothing else. No 'things never slow down', no 'the longer you wait the harder this gets', no 'what if all you had to do was show up and everything else was handled'.

The timing objection was real in substance — 'I have to wait till that happens', a house sale the prospect put at one to two months. None of the OD moves ran: no 'things never slow down', no 'the longer you wait the harder this gets', no 'the only thing you can control is right now'. The rep resolved a timing objection by lowering the entry price instead of collapsing the timeline.

A clean timing objection with a specific, credible date attached: 'I want to say by the end of June, I should be set to get on', 'I have two more months before I get commission', and 'I'm going have to wait on that for a little bit, until I'm a little better financially.' None of the OD moves ran. No 'things never slow down', no 'when does it actually become the right time', no 'the longer you wait the harder this gets'. And here, unusually, running the play would have been wrong anyway — the prospect's income genuinely does step change in two to three months, so the honest move was a firm diarised follow-up. That is broadly what happened, but it arrived after two payment links, a credit-card recommendation and a subscription sale rather than instead of them.

Fear of harm was present — 'they're not sure if me swinging around is the best idea.' The rep used a partial-value reframe and a good path-to-yes question ('what would be the route to getting you back to swinging stuff around?'), but ran none of the scripted OE moves: no certainty question, no bridge, no plane, no burned-before.

Correctly identified, nearly verbatim: 'Yeah, you're looking for certainty, essentially' — and the prospect confirmed it himself later ('You're right. It's certainty. That's what it is.'). But of the scripted moves only the naming ran. No pleasure-versus-pain question, no BRIDGE, no PLANE, no BURNED BEFORE, no 'how will you know if you never actually try'. The rep substituted his own comfort-zone material and a life-savings-on-a-mentor story, which was well received but is off-script and unrepeatable by another rep.

Two distinct doubts surfaced and neither got the play. The self-doubt behind the 8/10 — 'Because I know people, and I know myself' — is a fear-of-failure statement from a man who has just described a lifelong pattern of quitting, and the rep answered it with 'What gives you the confidence to say an 8?' rather than any part of Objection E. The BURNED BEFORE move was sitting right there and was never used. The second doubt was about the service: 'I have my doubts on 60 people. That's wild.' Neither the certainty question, the bridge, nor the plane analogy was attempted.

Run pre-emptively rather than in response, which is what makes it worth recording separately. At 00:19:13, before any offer or price existed, the rep constructed the fear frame around the prospect's just-disclosed condition: 'when it's really time for us to help you step into that version of you, that in itself is a fight or flight moment... are you going to listen to that voice... I'm going to push forward in spite of that feeling, or are you going to choose to continue the patterns that's not really served you well till now?' That is recognisably the spirit of Objection E — the bridge, the push-through-the-feeling move — but deployed as an inoculation rather than a rebuttal, and built from material the prospect had given him about an anxiety disorder. It worked: 'I'm all in.' Scored partial on execution and flagged on conduct.

Fear was present in two distinct forms and the rep worked both. Concrete fear of re-injury with a livelihood attached — 'I don't want to get injured again. I work for myself now, I have to go to work, I don't get sick pay' — and abstract self-doubt at the decision point: 'are you really ready for this? Can you commit to it? Are you going to do it? Or are you going to fail again?' Ran: a variant of the PLANE move using skydiving, the naming of fear as the universal blocker, 'that's probably the fear talking', 'At the precipice of making a decision like this, that voice grows louder' and the counter-voice framing. Not run: 'Would it be fair to say you're looking for certainty?', the BRIDGE, and above all BURNED BEFORE — which was written for exactly this prospect, who has been hurt by training twice and by a steroid injection once, and which was never used. The rep also closed the call by pre-empting future doubt: 'Over the next few days, that voice is going to grow louder... just remember that.'

Fear of injury was raised early and unprompted — 'my biggest risk to reaching my goals, I feel, is injury, and trying too hard' — with a concrete history behind it: he hurt his back doing calisthenics and lost weeks, and described the relapse spiral that follows. The rep did not engage with it when it landed but did address it later and well, tying the film-and-review loop to the prospect's own gun dog experience: 'it's the same thing that you did with your dog trainer, essentially.' None of the scripted moves ran — no certainty question, no BRIDGE, no PLANE, and no BURNED BEFORE, which was directly applicable.

Fear was named by both parties and is the true blocker on this call: 'my hesitation is, will I be able to do it with my little injuries?' and earlier, when asked what holds people back, 'Fear... Because I've lived it.' Ran: the fear-of-failure-or-success framing, the comfort-zone sequence, and the audit-and-no-rush reassurance. Not run: the certainty question, the BRIDGE, the PLANE, and most conspicuously BURNED BEFORE — 'if you got hurt in a relationship once, do you never trust again?' — which is the exact play for a man who has been physically hurt by training every four to five months for fifteen years. It was available and unused.

Fear was live and named by the prospect repeatedly — 'I think I live a life in fear, sometimes', 'the fear of failure or the fear of success', and the cold pool image. The PLANE move ran well: 'it's kind of like standing on an airplane ready to skydive when you haven't skydived before. And the longer you look down, guess what feeling grows stronger?'. The responsibility transfer landed ('who's responsible for actually taking that leap off the plane... despite the fear?' — 'me'). But the certainty question was never asked, the pleasure-versus-pain question was never asked, the BRIDGE and BURNED BEFORE moves never ran, and the rep started the FEAR acronym and abandoned it mid-sentence: 'it's an acronym for it, but it's not really coming to my mind at the moment'. Started and partly abandoned.

Doubt was live in two distinct forms and neither was addressed. First, efficacy doubt from direct experience: 'we did use a membership for my son, where one of them was actually online, like this was not helpful at all.' The BURNED BEFORE move exists in the playbook for precisely this and did not run. Second, and more importantly, he named his own decision criterion out loud — 'making sure that the movements are right, I'm not injuring myself. That's the key' — which is simultaneously the doubt to resolve and the programme's central feature. The weekly form-review loop had been described eight minutes earlier and was never connected to it.

'It's just scary' about putting $1,200 on the card is the trigger. The rep ran an off-script comfort-zone move and a long personal story about spending his life savings on a mentor and asking his father for advice — structurally the BRIDGE move, take the first step rather than see the whole other side. None of the scripted framings ran: no certainty question, no pleasure-versus-pain, no PLANE, no BURNED BEFORE, no 'how will you know if you never actually try'.

Doubt was live in two forms. The stated one, attributed to his wife, was 'is it going to work? Like, is it something that good to invest on it?', which the rep met correctly with the scripted closing move: 'how would you know that this is going to work or not if you don't actually try it?'. But the BURNED BEFORE move — which exists in the playbook precisely for this — was never run, despite the prospect having disclosed that he already lost about $1,000 to a coach who ignored him. The certainty question, the pleasure-versus-pain question, the BRIDGE and the PLANE were all absent. Started, and the most applicable move left on the table.

Fear of injury was stated outright as the reason he had never started kettlebells: 'I thought that looks like I'm going to screw something up on me and I don't want to get hurt.' No OE moves were used — no certainty question, no bridge, no plane. It was addressed obliquely and much later inside the philosophy pitch, via the first-month form-mastery framing. Effective in the room, but off-script, and it meant the fear was never separated from the four chronic joint complaints sitting underneath it.

objection_plays.trigger: I need to talk to my wife

instances.detail: Ran the isolate ('money out of it, you do feel confident this is what you want to do, right?'), the obstacle-preview ('what do you think she'll say?' → 'skeptical... sticker shock') and the deposit-with-refund fallback. Did NOT run 'is there any reason she would NOT want you stronger and less in pain?', 'is this genuinely needing her input or asking permission to bet on yourself?', or the 'this isn't a joint decision like buying a house' ownership move — the three moves that actually dislodge this objection. Instead he told an anecdote about stopping asking his own partner for spending approval, hedged twice with 'I'm not telling you to do this'.

'My missus would shoot me' and later 'I don't think I could swing that with Fife' are the objection in substance. The rep answered the first with a joke about the Yorkshire Dales and the second by conceding. He never asked whether the partner would object to him being leaner and more functional, never asked whose decision it actually is, and never offered the deposit-and-refund fallback he used on the Parker S. call the day before.

'I just need to confirm with my lady that it's cool' is the trigger in substance and none of the six OB moves ran. No money-aside isolate, no 'when you talk to her, what obstacles might come up?', no 'is there any reason she would NOT want you stronger?', no ownership challenge, and no deposit fallback. The rep's entire response was 'that's all good' followed by scheduling. Inconsistent with his own behaviour three days earlier on the Parker S. call, where he ran the isolate, the obstacle preview and the deposit against the same objection.

A textbook trigger with a hard number attached: 'my wife and I have this thing where we talk about it before... anything over a thousand dollars, we need to talk about it before.' Ran: the permission-versus-input distinction almost verbatim — 'is it just a situation where you're letting her know, hey honey, this is what I'm going to do for my health, or is it asking, hey honey, do you think I should do this?' — the obstacles question in substance, via the sticker-shock discussion, and the devil's-advocate refusal scenario: 'despite all of that, she says no. What do you feel like you're going to do?' Not run, and this is the important part: 'Money aside, do you personally feel this CAN get you to your goal?' and above all 'Is there any reason she would NOT want you stronger and less in pain?' — a move written for precisely this man, who has hidden fifteen years of pain from her and whose wife has just been given hiking boots so she can join him. The scripted fallback of a refundable deposit was also not used; the rep substituted the $1,200 trial, which does not clear the $1,000 household threshold that created the objection in the first place.

The play ran essentially end to end, in order. Personal conviction confirmed first ('money aside, there's nothing else that's stopping you'). Obstacles anticipated: 'when you guys typically speak about things like this, what do you feel like the potential obstacle could be?'. The would-she-object move: 'why do you feel like she'd want you to become your best self, become stronger?'. Permission-versus-input reframed onto him: 'who's actually responsible for this?' — 'Yeah, me.' And the stuck-path resolution ran exactly as scripted: a deposit plus a refund promise. So by the playbook this is a hit. Two things went beyond the script and should be reviewed as script rather than as rep error. First, an unevidenced closing claim: 'I've had this conversation 2,000 times, dude. You know, when anyone says they speak to their wife, I've never seen anyone come back.' Second, a direct push to pre-commit against his spouse's refusal — 'so even if she says like, hell no, you're still going to do it?' — repeated twice until he answered 'Probably.' Neither move is in the playbook and both are aimed at a 23-year-old who had said 'I'm new to the marriage.'

The clearest OB trigger in the batch — 'I have to discuss with my wife' and 'do you mind if I just have a conversation with my wife and then reach out to you on Monday?' The rep ran exactly one move from the play, and it was the last-resort fallback: put down a deposit, go talk to her, full refund if she says no. Every diagnostic move ahead of it was skipped — no 'money aside, do you personally feel this CAN get you to your goal', no 'when you talk to her, what obstacles might come up', no 'is there any reason she would NOT want you stronger and less in pain', no 'is this genuinely needing her input, or asking permission to bet on yourself', and no 'this isn't a joint decision like buying a house.' Jumping straight to the fallback converted a live objection into a rescheduled call and a refundable $100.

The most consequential miss on the call. 'I'm gonna wait till my wife comes tomorrow, I'm gonna see what she thinks too' arrived after the prospect had already reported her position — 'I told my wife yesterday, she's like, you're crazy. You're going to pay 6,000.' One move ran, 'What do you think she thinks?', drew a deflection, and the rep abandoned the subject and never returned to it. None of the remaining moves ran: no 'money aside, do you personally feel this CAN get you to your goal', no 'is there any reason she would NOT want you stronger and less in pain', no 'is this genuinely needing her input or asking permission to bet on yourself', no 'this isn't a joint decision like buying a house', and no deposit fallback. He spent the following five minutes hunting for a hidden blocker that had already been named out loud.

Played through to the best available outcome. Got her name, confirmed she knew about the call, asked what could prevent them moving forward, and ran the permission-versus-FYI question near-verbatim: 'when you speak to Gabrielle, is that a, like a, when I say this with respect, like a permission thing, or is it just like an FYI kind of thing?' The prospect then brought her onto the call live, she asked her own substantive questions and approved. NOT run: 'Is there any reason she would NOT want you stronger and less in pain?' and 'This isn't a joint decision like buying a house.' Skipping those was the right call — bringing her in beat working around her.

The most complete play run anywhere in this batch. Ran: is she on the call and in the house, got her name, checked she was supportive ('is she receptive? Is she supportive of you actually stepping into your higher self?'), the social-proof story about the Oklahoma prospect whose wife joined and signed up, the invitation for Hannah to join and ask questions, the precedent question ('Have you guys made a decision like this before, when it comes to this amount?' — a bathroom remodel) and whose idea that was, the blocker isolate ('what is the main potential that could prevent you from doing this? Is it just the finances?'), and finally the scripted stuck-fallback: deposit now, talk to her, full refund if she says no. NOT run: 'Is there any reason she would NOT want you stronger and less in pain?', 'Is this genuinely needing her input — or asking permission to bet on yourself?', and 'This isn't a joint decision like buying a house. Is that responsibility hers or yours?' Those three challenge moves were skipped in favour of accommodating the partner, which is a defensible read on a couple who have only just combined finances but is not the script.

Triggered clearly and twice — 'I can't just pull that trigger by myself without talking to my wife' and later the household rule, 'we have a rule that we talk about things that are, like, over $100 purchase.' Not one OB move ran. He never asked her name, never asked whether she would be receptive, never asked whether it was permission or an FYI, never invited her onto the call, and never offered the deposit-and-refund fallback. He ran this play thoroughly on two other calls in the same batch, so it is a lapse rather than a capability gap — though with $4-5K liquid the deposit fallback would arguably have been the wrong thing to reach for.

"my wife is also part of the company holder I would have to ask her." The rep ran most of the play cleanly: isolated with 'money aside do you feel like we can actually get you to where you want to go', asked her name ("I don't want to call her your wife"), asked what she would say to the €5,100 through the business, and ran the permission-vs-FYI frame ("is it more of like a, hey, just letting you know... or is it like a permission thing"). Not run: 'is there any reason she would NOT want you stronger', and the deposit-with-refund fallback.

The only objection play in the batch played through to its scripted terminal move. Trigger at 00:24:29. Ran: asked her name to personalise it ('What's your wife's name? I don't want to call her your wife' — 'Lauren'), asked whether she is supportive of the journey, established she had not been told anything yet, ran the two-reactions framing to elicit the likely obstacle ('How do you feel like she would react to that?' — 'the money piece of it would be probably the biggest sticking point'), isolated personal commitment twice, and then closed the scripted fallback exactly as written: a refundable deposit with a full refund if she says no, plus a booked follow-up. The prospect paid it inside a minute. Not run: 'is there any reason she would NOT want you stronger and less in pain', the permission-versus-input challenge, and the 'this isn't a joint decision like buying a house' ownership move — reasonably omitted given the prospect framed the decision in explicitly joint and faith terms.

unmet_themes.blurb: One-to-one time, live form checks, technique correction, in-person contact. A request for a higher-touch version of what is already sold.

unmet_themes.label: Cheaper, shorter or more flexible terms
unmet_themes.blurb: Not a product request — a request to buy the same product differently. Almost always a positioning or packaging question.

unmet_themes.label: Nutrition and diet

unmet_themes.label: Evidence it works for someone like them
unmet_themes.blurb: Case studies, results, track record — proof at their age, their body type or their starting point. A trust request, not a product one.

unmet_themes.blurb: Practical delivery: what they own, where they train, when they can do it. Cheap to solve and often already solved.

unmet_themes.blurb: Train with a spouse, partner or family member, or get a household rate. A packaging question the offer has no answer for.

unmet_themes.label: Everything else
unmet_themes.blurb: Requests that matched no theme — one-offs, and the genuinely idiosyncratic.

pain_groups.blurb: Injury, medical constraint and age. The pain is physical and already diagnosed — they are not guessing that something is wrong.

pain_groups.label: It is costing them outside the gym

pain_groups.label: Everything else
pain_groups.blurb: Categories outside the named groups, including the uncategorised bucket.

goal_groups.label: Still be doing this at seventy
goal_groups.blurb: Function, mobility and staying unbroken. The dominant want in this corpus and the one the offer is actually built for.

goal_groups.label: Look the part
goal_groups.blurb: Fat loss, muscle and appearance. Stated less often than longevity but rarely absent underneath it.

goal_groups.label: Become someone who shows up
goal_groups.blurb: Consistency, confidence and being the example at home. An identity goal, not an outcome one — and the one that sells a year, not a month.

goal_groups.label: Perform at something
goal_groups.blurb: Strength, endurance and a sport or hobby they want to be better at.

goal_groups.label: Make it fit a full life
goal_groups.blurb: Convenience above all: it has to survive a real week.

goal_groups.label: Everything else
goal_groups.blurb: Categories outside the named groups, including the uncategorised bucket.

objection_groups.blurb: No stated blocker, just deferral. The hardest group to resolve because there is nothing concrete to answer.

objection_groups.label: Someone else decides
objection_groups.blurb: A spouse, a partner or unresolved doubt about the provider. The decision is not the prospect's alone to make on the call.

objection_groups.label: Everything else
objection_groups.blurb: Objections that did not fall into a named group, including the uncategorised bucket.

themes.label: Prices outside the sanctioned list
themes.blurb: Tiers and figures presented as standard that do not appear in the documented offer — improvised three-month, one-month and trial structures, priced live on the call.

themes.label: Loaded training sold without clinician clearance
themes.blurb: A prospect disclosed an injury, condition or active treatment and was sold loaded or ballistic kettlebell work anyway, with no clearance sought and no stop rule anywhere in the process.

themes.label: Payment plan terms differ call to call
themes.blurb: Instalment totals, deposits and differential-credit mechanics stated differently to different prospects, and often with the total never stated at all.

themes.label: Disclosed condition, no screening question
themes.blurb: A medical disclosure passed without a single follow-up question. There is no screening step in the script for it to have failed.

themes.label: Unqualified clinical claims
themes.blurb: A rep asserting a medical or rehabilitative outcome they are not qualified to promise — that the programme will fix, heal or resolve a diagnosed condition.

themes.label: One file, two calls — or the wrong name on it
themes.blurb: Drive files containing two unrelated sales calls back to back, and titles naming a different prospect than the transcript. Anything counting or joining on files is wrong by this amount.

themes.label: Speaker labels cannot be trusted
themes.blurb: Diarisation errors and mislabelled speakers, including one label that names the wrong rep entirely. Rep attribution has to come from folder and content, never the transcript label.

themes.label: The guarantee is not a fixed thing
themes.blurb: Refund and guarantee language varies by whoever is on the call, when it is mentioned at all.

themes.label: Recording and disclosure gaps
themes.blurb: Calls recorded without a stated disclosure, third parties captured incidentally, and claims made without the qualifying context.

themes.label: Documented steps skipped after the sale
themes.blurb: Agreements never signed live, onboarding steps missed, written terms promised and never sent. The process exists; it is not being run.

themes.label: Pressure and card-on-file tactics
themes.blurb: Taking a card from prospects who said they could not pay, deposits framed as commitment devices, and manager instruction to do so.

themes.label: A policy stated, then reversed
themes.blurb: Rules given as fixed to a prospect and abandoned within hours when the deal was at risk, or contradicted in the same breath. The pattern says there was no policy.

themes.label: Definitions that flatter the pipeline
themes.blurb: Disposition rules confining 'lost' to explicit refusals, so everything unresolved lands in follow-up and the pipeline never shrinks.

themes.label: Calls missing from the corpus entirely
themes.blurb: Selling calls absent while their onboarding call is present, and role-played sequences that read as genuine to any content classifier. Both bias the denominator.

themes.label: Advice on the prospect's finances
themes.blurb: Steering purchases around divorce settlements, tax write-offs and invoice descriptions. Not a training issue.

themes.label: Prospects profiled by who they are
themes.blurb: Country of origin, accent and demographic used as a proxy for ability to pay, with harder qualification prescribed on that basis.

themes.label: Dietary advice given alongside medication
themes.blurb: Fasting windows, eating protocols and supplement guidance offered to prospects on active medication, by people not qualified to give it.

themes.label: Recording stopped at the moment of payment
themes.blurb: The transaction and any terms stated during it are absent from the corpus. This biases the close rate in both directions and cannot be resolved without a CRM join.

themes.label: Coached pressure technique
themes.blurb: Refusing to accept a stated answer, holding the position until the prospect complies, enlarging their goal to enlarge the sale, and keeping buyers on the phone until they pay. Coached, not improvised.

themes.label: Unverified numbers used as proof
themes.blurb: Client counts and result figures presented as the primary trust asset with nothing behind them, in place of specific evidence.

themes.label: Personal data captured on the recording
themes.blurb: Card numbers, addresses and contact details dictated onto a call and preserved in the stored transcript.

themes.label: Everything else
themes.blurb: Flags that matched no theme — the genuine long tail, reported rather than dropped so the map can be judged.
